Context/Background:
Intraductal papillary neoplasms (IPNs),  including intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs), intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasms (IOPNs), and intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasms (ITPNs), are clinically detectable macroscopic non-invasive cyst-forming lesions, some of which progress to invasive pancreatic cancer. Proteins and glycoproteins have proven to be useful clinical biomarkers for classifying cyst-forming neoplasms in the pancreas.Here, we used proteomics and glycoproteomics to characterize a series of histologically and genetically well-characterized surgically resected IPNs, including IPMNs and IOPNs.

Our analysis included 69 IPNs (64 IPMNs and 5 IOPNs), 76 macro-dissected grossly normal duct tissues (NDs, with 32 of the 76 NDs coming from the same resection specimens as the IPNs), and 32 cyst fluid samples (22 from matched IPMN patients, 3 matched IOPN patients, 2 from unrelated IPMN patients, and 5 other cysts).
Prompt: We applied proteomics-based NMF subtyping strategies to the IPMNs and PDACs to explore tumor heterogeneities and reveal progression features. This analysis showed three clusters, NMF 1 was entirely composed of PDACs. NMF 2 included some PDACs and some IPMNs, while NMF 3 was almost entirely composed of IPMNs with only one PDAC. Most (75%) IPMNs with an associated PDAC were clustered in NMF 2. Use the feature genes in each of the NMF clusters and pairwise comparison between clusters to interpret the differences between NMF clusters and provide a summary of functional and clinical implications.
output_text:
Introduction/Context  
Proteomics and glycoproteomics were applied to 69 intraductal papillary neoplasms (64 IPMNs, 5 IOPNs), 76 macroscopically normal duct tissues, and 32 cyst fluids to define three proteomic-based NMF clusters spanning IPMNs and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDACs). NMF 1 comprises only PDACs; NMF 3 is almost exclusively IPMNs; NMF 2 is a mixed “transitional” state containing PDACs and IPMNs (including 75% of IPMNs with associated PDAC). Feature genes and differential‐expression (DE) comparisons between clusters were mined to elucidate underlying biology and potential progression‐relevant pathways. For details not specified here (e.g. sample replicates), the source remains “not specified.”

Keywords

• Vesicle trafficking  
• Heme metabolism

• UBA6  
• APOM  
• ARPC5

Summary  
NMF 3 (predominantly IPMNs) shows upregulation of secretion and exocytosis programs (Pancreatic/Salivary secretion; Regulation of Exocytosis; RAB geranylgeranylation) and downregulation of complement/coagulation, protein metabolic processes, and broad immune pathways. This secretory/metabolic phenotype suggests an active vesicle‐driven mucin export and altered immune surveillance in non-invasive lesions. NMF 2 (mixed IPMN/PDAC) demonstrates strong ECM remodeling and focal adhesion upregulation (Focal adhesion, ECM–receptor interaction, PI3K-Akt) alongside heme metabolism and redox processes (Heme metabolism, H₂O₂ catabolism). This transitional cluster likely represents lesions acquiring stromal remodeling and increased oxidative stress, hallmarks of early invasion. NMF 1 (PDAC only) is enriched in cytoskeletal reprogramming (Arp2/3 complex, actin polymerization) and innate immune signaling (IFIT3) based on feature genes and DE between NMF 1 vs NMF 2, indicative of a mesenchymal, motile, and immune-evasive phenotype.  

Targeted (Keyword‐Guided) Subset  
Focusing on “Exocytosis” in NMF 3 GSEA results recovers Regulation Of Exocytosis (GO:0017157; RAB27B, RAB3D). “Matrix” in NMF 2 GSEA highlights Extracellular Matrix Organization (Reactome; COL4A1, COL6A1, COL6A2, TNXB). These pathway‐level signals align directly with the chosen keywords and candidate genes, reinforcing the cluster‐specific biology of secretion in IPMNs and ECM remodeling in transitional lesions.  

Key Genes/Proteins (leading edge)

| RAB27B   | Up in NMF 3 | Vesicle docking/exocytosis            | Regulation Of Exocytosis; Pancreatic secretion |  
| NDUFA4   | Up in NMF 3 | Complex IV subunit driving OXPHOS     | Oxidative Phosphorylation (Hallmark); OxPhos (KEGG) |  
| COL6A1   | Up in NMF 2 | ECM protein, cell–matrix adhesion     | Focal adhesion; ECM–receptor interaction |  

Down:  
| Gene     | Direction | Role/Function                         | Pathway(s)                         |  
|----------|-----------|---------------------------------------|------------------------------------|  
| C3       | Down in NMF 3 | Central complement component          | Complement and coagulation cascades |  
| SERPINA1 | Down in NMF 3 | Serine protease inhibitor, acute phase | Complement; Coagulation             |  

Comparisons & Confidence  
• Secretory/exocytosis and mitochondrial programs are IPMN-specific (NMF 3) and not seen in NMF 2/1 (high confidence).  
• ECM/focal adhesion upregulation is prominent in NMF 2 but not in pure IPMN (NMF 3) or PDAC (NMF 1) (moderate confidence).  
• Actin cytoskeleton/immune-evasion programs are unique to PDAC (NMF 1) (high confidence).  

Clinical & Therapeutic Implications  
• NMF 3’s mucin secretion signature suggests targeting vesicular trafficking or mucin biosynthesis to intercept IPMN progression.  
• NMF 2’s ECM remodeling and oxidative stress programs indicate potential benefit from stroma-modulating or redox-targeted therapies in early invasion.  
• NMF 1’s cytoskeletal and immune signatures point toward anti-motility agents and immune checkpoint strategies in established PDAC.  

Next Steps & Clarification  
1. Validate whether cell‐cycle and replication pathways (e.g., DNA synthesis) are altered across clusters—DE results did not highlight these at FDR < 0.05 (not observed).  
2. Assess stress‐response pathways (e.g., heat-shock proteins) in NMF 2 vs 3; hydrogen peroxide catabolism was up in NMF 2, suggesting oxidative stress adaptation.  
3. Integrate glycoproteomics to confirm whether secreted glycoproteins track with the exocytosis signature in NMF 3 cyst fluids.  
4. Map spatial distribution of these clusters in resected tissues to link proteomic subtypes with histopathology and patient outcomes.
